title: Yet sins are not equal—against the Stoic parity of vices
source_text: V. Caeterum quamvis contendant peccatum quodlibet ex se mortem aeternam mereri, & rejectionem a Dei amore & benevolentia, multum tamen ab eo absunt, ut cum Stoicis sentiant peccata omnia paria & aequalia esse. Si quidem fatentur inter peccatum & peccatum magnum discrimen reperiri; & unum altero longe gravius & atrocius esse: adeoque licet peccatis singulis aeterna quaedam poena respondeat, inter peccatorum poenas varios tamen esse gradus, & unum altero longe mitius puniendum esse. Prout docet Evangelium servum illum, qui cognita heri sui voluntate, illam non executus est, pluribus & durioribus plagis caedendum fore, quam illum qui eam ignorans violavit, licet & iste non sit hoc impune laturus.
pass_a_gloss: But although they contend that any sin whatever of itself merits eternal death and rejection from God’s love and goodwill, they are nevertheless far from thinking with the Stoics that all sins are alike and equal. For they confess that a great difference is found between sin and sin; and that one is far graver and more atrocious than another: and so, although some eternal penalty answers to each several sin, yet among the penalties of sinners there are various degrees, and one is to be punished far more mildly than another. As the Gospel teaches that that servant who, knowing his master’s will, did not perform it, shall be beaten with many and harder stripes than he who violated it in ignorance, though he too shall not go unpunished for this.
pass_b_english: Intrinsic desert of death does not make all sins Stoic equals—gravity and penalty have degrees.
Luke’s knowing and ignorant servants mark unequal stripes even where none go free.
